assessment.nobel_worthiness: The heterogeneous-firm framework changed how trade economists think about who gains from trade. It brought within-industry reallocation, selection into exporting and productivity-driven gains into a tractable general-equilibrium model, and it spawned a large body of empirical and policy work. The transformation of a field is clear and measured by the usual standards of method, scope and durability.
assessment.attribution: Melitz (2003) is the central contribution. Helpman's work on firm-level trade, including the later Helpman–Melitz–Yeaple contributions, is the natural complement. Redding is a major contributor to quantitative spatial and trade work, but his role is more extensive than foundational. Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum are not on this ballot and are an obvious attribution issue.
assessment.maturity: More than two decades of confirmation across many datasets and countries, and the framework is now textbook material. The timing is mature.
uncertainties: Prior trade recognition (Krugman 2008) may reduce appetite for another trade prize.
Whether the credit should be limited to two people, or should include Bernard–Eaton–Jensen–Kortum, who are not credited on this ballot.
Quantitative gains-from-trade magnitudes remain debated.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: A coherent, influential body of work on how technology, tasks and trade exposure reshape labour demand and wage inequality. It runs from the skill-biased change literature through the task framework to local labour-market effects of import competition. It affects both academic research and the public debate on globalisation and automation. It also speaks to the present concerns about technological change and the costs of adjustment for displaced workers.
assessment.attribution: Katz's skill-demand and returns-to-skill work, Autor's task approach and the Autor–Dorn–Hanson China-shock studies are distinct contributions. Acemoglu's closely related work was already recognised in 2024, and Goldin (2023) and Card (2021) were recognised in neighbouring areas. A three-person recognition of Autor, Katz and Hanson is the plausible cut; Dorn is a real co-author on the trade-shock work.
assessment.maturity: The foundational papers are 15 to 30 years old, and the evidence has been extended and tested against alternative explanations. The matter is mature enough, though debate on mechanisms continues.
uncertainties: Overlap with already-recognised neighbours (Acemoglu, Goldin, Card) may lower the marginal case.
Exact weighting between the task/skill literature and the trade-shock literature is uncertain.
Some of the reduced-form trade-shock evidence is sensitive to design choices.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Long-run top-income series built from tax records opened up a field. They reset what economists know about the historical evolution of inequality and led to new data infrastructure such as the World Inequality Database. The contribution is substantially one of measurement, built from archival sources, and it has changed both research agendas and public discussion.
assessment.attribution: Piketty–Saez top-income work is the core. Zucman's wealth and offshore-wealth contributions are significant but more recent and, in some respects, more contested. Atkinson, who was a pioneer of this approach, is deceased and cannot share a prize. Capital in the Twenty-First Century's theoretical claims (r>g) are less secure than the data work, so the prize case rests on the measurement.
assessment.maturity: The top-income series date from about 2003 and have been replicated and extended across countries. The wealth-tax and offshore-wealth strands are younger.
uncertainties: Debate over the measurement of top incomes (e.g. the treatment of retained earnings, transfers and taxes) and over the validity of the r>g inference.
The prize may be judged on measurement or on theory, with different consequences for who is credited.
Policy prominence could make the assessment contested.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Resource misallocation across firms is a quantitative explanation of cross-country income and TFP differences that connects micro-level distortions to aggregate growth. Hsieh and Klenow (2009) made it a standard approach in growth and development accounting, and it is widely used by researchers and policy institutions. It also connects directly to long-run comparative growth.
assessment.attribution: Hsieh–Klenow is the central contribution. Restuccia–Rogerson and Restuccia–Hsieh work are closely related, so a three-way split is possible. Banerjee–Duflo and Jones are relevant adjacent credit. The ballot's selection of three is a plausible but not unique credited set.
assessment.maturity: About 15 years of replication and extension, and the framework is now standard in macro-development. The timing is reasonably mature.
uncertainties: The measured gaps from misallocation are sensitive to measurement error and to modelling assumptions on markups and adjustment costs.
Credit split with Restuccia (and Rogerson, who is not credited) is unresolved.
Recent Nobel recognition of growth (2018, 2024, 2025) may reduce room for this topic.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Population-scale administrative data brought new precision to intergenerational mobility. It documented large geographic variation in opportunity and developed quasi-experimental estimates of neighbourhood causal effects. The data-construction effort is at the scale a Nobel committee notes, and it has given policy debates empirical grounding.
assessment.attribution: Chetty is the central figure and Hendren is the author of key causal-neighbourhood work. Friedman and Katz are significant co-authors. Chetty's wider body of work also appears in public economics (B041), so the credit is spread across several ballots. Attribution within this large collaborative group is not clear-cut.
assessment.maturity: The main results date from 2014 to 2022. Replication and long-term follow-up are still accumulating, so the case is less mature than the older candidates.
uncertainties: Long-term persistence of neighbourhood effects and the interpretation of geographic variation remain under study.
Chetty's work could be recognised through a different ballot item, with consequences for how credit is allocated.
Younger work implies a possible later timing.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Persson–Tabellini and Besley developed formal and empirical political economics, relating constitutions, electoral rules, state capacity and fiscal policy to economic outcomes. It is a broad, integrated research programme that opened up an area connecting economics with political science, and it is widely used. Recent prizes (2024) on institutions and growth are adjacent but distinct.
assessment.attribution: The credited trio matches the established core of the field, with Persson–Tabellini jointly and Besley's work on state capacity and accountability. Acemoglu and Robinson, recognised in 2024, are close neighbours, so the overlap must be weighed.
assessment.maturity: About 30 years of development with extensive empirical follow-up. The case is mature.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2024 prize on institutions may weaken the incremental case.
Empirical identification of constitutional effects relies on cross-country comparisons, which have well-known limits.
Possible conflict of interest involving committee members connected to the field, which is disclosed but not adjudicated here.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The New Keynesian framework, built from nominal rigidities, rule-based monetary policy and the microfounded policy analysis, became the working model of central banks. Its practical influence is large and the theoretical consolidation is coherent.
assessment.attribution: Attribution is the main difficulty. The ballot lists eight names, and credit is spread across Calvo (pricing), Taylor (rules and staggered contracts), Woodford (the integrated framework), Galí, Gertler, Clarida and others. Any trio omits significant contributors, and Christiano–Eichenbaum–Evans and Smets–Wouters add a separate medium-scale DSGE strand. Fischer is a further early contributor who is not listed.
assessment.maturity: Three decades of use in practice, and the framework has been tested through the 2008 crisis and the inflation surge of 2021–23, which exposed both strengths and weaknesses.
uncertainties: The post-2021 inflation episode and heterogeneous-agent critiques (B031) affect the verdict.
The three-person cap makes the attribution contested.
Recent prizes in macroeconomics (2022 Bernanke et al. on banking) may influence timing.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Dynamic panel GMM estimators (Arellano–Bond, Arellano–Bover/Blundell–Bond) are among the most-used tools in applied economics and are central to empirical growth, firm and labour analysis. The contribution is methodological, and its value shows in how widely it is applied.
assessment.attribution: Arellano–Bond (1991) and Blundell–Bond (1998) define the contribution, with Arellano–Bover (1995) as a closely related precursor. Bover is not credited here. Blundell's work on labour and structural models also appears in B006, so credit across ballots overlaps.
assessment.maturity: Three decades of use. The limitations are well known, including instrument proliferation and weak-instrument problems in persistent series.
uncertainties: The committee has recently favoured identification and causal-inference methods, and it is unclear whether estimation methods of this kind would be treated similarly.
Known weaknesses of the estimators, including many-instrument bias, may be weighed against the case.
The overlap between Blundell's contributions across several ballots complicates the credit.
